questions.stem: Carl, 54, has type 2 diabetes and 4 months of burning retrosternal pain after dinner. He mentions it is worse if he walks to the shops straight after eating. You are taking the history in general practice. Which follow-up question best separates stable angina from reflux?
options: Does the pain feel burning rather than heavy or tight, and linger for an hour or more?
Is the pain worse after a large or heavy meal?
Does it come on with exertion alone and settle within minutes of rest?
Does the pain spread to your arm, jaw or neck?
questions.why: Angina is brought on by exertion and settles within minutes of rest. Carl's pain does not start with tennis on its own and lasts about 30 minutes whatever he does. How the pain relates to exertion and to rest is the key discriminator.
notes: How patients describe the pain is unreliable: angina can be described as burning, especially in people with diabetes, so this question cannot separate the two.
Angina can also be worse after a heavy meal, so a link with meals does not distinguish it from reflux.
Many patients with angina have no radiation, so a 'no' answer does not exclude it. Duration and response to rest discriminate better.

questions.stem: Carl, 54, has daily typical reflux symptoms with no alarm features. His ECG is normal and his Hb and ferritin are normal. Alongside lifestyle advice (smaller, earlier, less spicy meals, raising the head of the bed, weight loss), you start drug treatment in general practice. Which regimen is most appropriate?
options: Esomeprazole 20 mg orally once daily, 30 to 60 minutes before a meal, for 4 to 8 weeks
Esomeprazole 40 mg orally twice daily, 30 minutes before meals, for 12 weeks, then stop
Omeprazole 20 mg orally once daily at bedtime, continued long term
Famotidine 20 mg orally twice daily for 2 weeks, then stop if improved
questions.why: First-line treatment for troublesome GORD is a standard-dose PPI once daily, 30 to 60 minutes before a meal, for 4 to 8 weeks. The trial is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Then step down to the lowest effective dose.
notes: A high dose twice daily is for when standard-dose treatment fails or for severe oesophagitis. Taking it with meals rather than before them also makes it work less well.
A dose at bedtime on an empty stomach misses the meal-stimulated proton pumps. Starting with indefinite treatment, rather than a trial and then step-down, is not appropriate.
An H2 antagonist is an alternative but works less well than a PPI for daily troublesome reflux, and 2 weeks is too short to judge a response.

questions.stem: Carl, 54, gets reflux mainly after a large curry at 8 pm, and it is worse when he lies down at 9.30 pm. He has type 2 diabetes but no early satiety or vomiting. In most patients with GORD like Carl, what is the main mechanism that lets gastric contents reflux into the oesophagus?
options: Persistently low resting pressure of the lower oesophageal sphincter throughout the day
Transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations triggered by gastric distension
Gastric acid hypersecretion driven by raised serum gastrin
Delayed gastric emptying from diabetic autonomic neuropathy
questions.why: Transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations, which are not triggered by swallowing, cause most reflux episodes. Stretch of the proximal stomach after a big meal sets them off through a vagal reflex. This is why large, late meals make reflux worse.
notes: A low resting sphincter pressure matters mainly in severe or erosive disease and in scleroderma. It is not the main mechanism in most patients.
Most patients with GORD secrete a normal amount of acid. Hypergastrinaemia with hypersecretion suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and nothing here points to it.
Gastroparesis can contribute in some patients with diabetes, but Carl has no early satiety or vomiting, and it is not the main mechanism of GORD.

questions.stem: Carl, 54, is centrally obese and has nocturnal reflux. At gastroscopy he is found to have a small sliding hiatus hernia, in which the gastro-oesophageal junction moves up above the diaphragm. Which structure normally forms the external part of the antireflux barrier around the lower oesophagus?
options: Left crus of the diaphragm, at the level of T12
Median arcuate ligament, at the level of T12
Central tendon of the diaphragm, at the level of T8
Right crus of the diaphragm, at the level of T10
questions.why: Fibres of the right crus of the diaphragm loop around the oesophageal hiatus at T10 and act as an external sphincter that adds to the lower oesophageal sphincter. In a sliding hiatus hernia the junction is pulled away from the crus, which weakens the barrier.
notes: The left crus is the smaller crus and does not classically form the oesophageal hiatus. T12 is the level of the aortic hiatus.
The median arcuate ligament joins the two crura in front of the aorta at T12. It forms the aortic hiatus, not the oesophageal one.
The central tendon at T8 contains the opening for the inferior vena cava, not the opening for the oesophagus.
